title: Asiya's arms
hookLine: Pharaoh's wife finds the baby and says: a joy for me and you, do not kill him
carry: a good heart in a hard house

cards: A gentle parent raised by a harsh one. A coworker who stays decent in an office where nobody else bothers. Kindness doesn't always come from the house a person is in; sometimes they carry it in themselves.
The river carries the chest downstream, and where does it wash up? Of all the places in Egypt, at Pharaoh's own palace. His household lifts it from the water.
Inside is a baby boy, exactly the kind Pharaoh has ordered killed. Then a woman steps forward, between the baby and the man who gives the orders.

teach.b: Surah al-Qasas again. Pharaoh's household picks the baby up, and his wife says: a delight of the eye for me and for you.
Do not kill him. Perhaps he will be of use to us, or we may take him as a son. Delight of the eye is qurratu 'ayn, literally coolness of the eye.

One old explanation: in a hot land, a cool eye is a happy one, resting on something it loves. She looks at a baby her husband has sentenced to death, calls him her delight to his face, and adds: do not kill him.
The Qur'an doesn't give her name. Muslim tradition calls her Asiya, and honors her. Her faith shows up later, in Surah at-Tahrim, where the Qur'an holds her up as an example for believers.

teach.h: A HOME WITH YOU IN THE GARDEN.
teach.b: She prays: my Lord, build for me a home with You in the Garden, and save me from Pharaoh and his deeds. The queen of Egypt, in a palace, asking for a different house.
And the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, in a hadith in Bukhari, named her among the women who reached perfection, alongside Maryam, the mother of 'Isa.
Two women in two very different houses, both remembered for a heart that stayed turned toward Allah, whatever the walls around it.
So the child who will one day stand against Pharaoh grows up in Pharaoh's house, held by Pharaoh's wife. The rescue walked in through the front door.

how: Muslims honor Asiya, the wife of Pharaoh, as a woman of faith the Qur'an itself holds up as an example, and some recite her prayer from Surah at-Tahrim in times of hardship.

o: the arms of a fisherman who pulled the chest ashore
the arms of a palace nurse who fed the baby Musa

games.q: what's inside the story — tap the pairs.
p: coolness of the eye: a delight

s: the Qur'an names Pharaoh's wife as Asiya
the Qur'an calls her the wife of Pharaoh. the name Asiya comes from Muslim tradition.
qurratu 'ayn literally means coolness of the eye
one old explanation: in a hot land, a cool eye is a happy one.
the Qur'an holds up Pharaoh's wife as an example for believers
in Surah at-Tahrim, with her prayer for a home with Allah in the Garden.

games.q: you're in Pharaoh's household. a chest is pulled from the river with a baby boy inside, the kind Pharaoh has ordered killed. what do you do?
o: hand him over. orders are orders.
say he's a delight, and ask Pharaoh not to kill him.
send him back down the river.
games.why: Pharaoh's wife says: a delight of the eye for me and for you. do not kill him. the future prophet grows up in the house of the man he'll one day stand against.

practice: Think of who around you has the least power: a child, a new hire, the quiet one who gets talked over in the group chat, an animal, an elderly neighbor.
Picture one of them, and a moment when you might be the one who says, do not, one sentence out loud when it counts: don't interrupt them, don't leave them out, don't make the joke at their expense.
If you pray, ask for a steady voice.

wordCard.voice: Asiya's arms: the wife of Pharaoh, who held the baby her husband wanted dead and said, do not kill him.

orig.note: Arabic, from Qur'an 28:9: "coolness of the eye," a delight — what Asiya called the baby.

carryVoice: Your line: a good heart in a hard house. Asiya kept one, in Pharaoh's own palace. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 3411 (many men reached perfection, and of women only Maryam and Asiya)
